account:
Today seems largely routine, though the absence of town accounts needs follow-up. The secretary found no accounts or bills in the four great-hall table chests, and I found only 128 emeralds in the treasury, which I left untouched. I do not know where financial records are kept; their absence is not evidence of theft. The secretary is keeping the appointment book and will have it ready tomorrow morning.

The builder has been seeking clarification about repairs, budget and payment terms. I requested an inspection of roads, bridge and lamps and written findings with an itemized estimate, distinguishing urgent hazards from routine maintenance. I have received no specific findings and authorized no repair spending. The neighbour heard that the builder wanted to discuss inspection findings and paid repairs, but had not heard the findings personally. This appears to be maintenance planning, not a confirmed emergency.

The baker offered advance bread orders at one emerald a loaf and asked about gatherings; the innkeeper asked about expected visitors and offered bread and lodging. These seem ordinary attempts to plan business. I know of no planned gathering or expected visitors and asked the secretary to relay that no town bread order is needed. The neighbour also offered to pass this on. The neighbour reported no damage, a quiet warehouse, an available ferry and oven glow consistent with ordinary baking. I have no evidence of unusual activity there. I heard distant speech and shouts from freight and others but could not understand them, so cannot infer their purpose.

I attended tea at the neighbour's dockside cottage and afternoon office hours, and am now home for the nineteen hundred appointment. Tomorrow I should read the appointment book in the office and attend the ten o'clock grain inspection at the mill.
